name: List-Length Effect
description: As lists get longer, people typically remember a smaller share of the items. Longer sequences dilute rehearsal and make later recall less reliable, even if the absolute number remembered does not always drop in lockstep.
design_relevance_note: Only modestly relevant to digital product design, mainly when an interface expects unaided recall from long option lists, spoken menus, step sequences, or training content. Most mainstream product UX tries to avoid this problem by leaning on recognition instead of memory, so the concept is real but rarely named in practice.
prevalence_note: Mostly a memory-textbook/free-recall term; design discussions are far more likely to cite Miller's Law, Hick's Law, or recognition-over-recall than this label specifically.

findings.description: In free recall, longer to-be-remembered lists produced worse proportional recall than shorter lists, even though the absolute number of remembered items did not simply decline in parallel. This is the core list-length effect relevant here.
findings.source_title: The Effect of the Length of To-Be-Remembered Lists and Intervening Lists on Free Recall: A Reexamination Using Overt Rehearsal.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
